title: 1 Samuel 29:1–5
context: As the Philistine armies gather at Aphek, the Philistine commanders object to David marching with them, fearing he will turn against them in battle and recalling the song about his victories.

verses.text: Now the Philistines gathered together all their armies to Aphek; and the Israelites encamped by the spring which is in Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines gather at Aphek, and Israel camps by the spring in Jezreel. Arminian readers see the narrative returning to David’s dilemma just before the decisive battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the story picking up the thread left in 28:1–2. The location notes show the armies drawing close and the pressure on David reaching its height.

verses.text: The lords of the Philistines passed on by hundreds and by thousands; and David and his men passed on in the rear with Achish.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistine lords pass in review, with David and his men at the rear with Achish. Arminian readers see David apparently committed to marching against Israel, a situation of his own making.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David in an awkward and dangerous place. The narrator presents the scene without revealing David’s inner intentions, increasing the suspense.

verses.text: Then the princes of the Philistines said, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish said to the princes of the Philistines, “Isn’t this David, the servant of Saul the king of Israel, who has been with me these days, or rather these years? I have found no fault in him since he fell away until today.”
verses.arminianNotes: The princes ask, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish answers, “I have found no fault in him since he fell away until today.” Arminian readers see Achish’s trust resting on David’s earlier deception.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the irony of Achish defending David as loyal. The princes’ question exposes the suspicion that Achish has not recognized.

verses.text: But the princes of the Philistines were angry with him; and the princes of the Philistines said to him, “Make the man return, that he may go back to his place where you have appointed him, and let him not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For with what should this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Should it not be with the heads of these men?
verses.arminianNotes: The princes demand, “Make the man return … lest in the battle he become an adversary to us.” Arminian readers see Philistine suspicion that turns out to protect David from a terrible choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence working through the princes’ distrust. Readers in both traditions commonly see David spared from fighting Israel by means he did not arrange.

verses.text: Isn’t this David, of whom people sang to one another in dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”
verses.arminianNotes: They recall the song, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” Arminian readers see David’s past reputation now working in his favor by disqualifying him from the battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the song of 1 Samuel 18:7 resurfacing at a decisive moment. David’s earlier victories, once a source of Saul’s envy, now keep him out of a conflict with his own people.
